papers.title: Automated detection, morphometric measurement, and size-class determination of harbor seals (Phoca vitulina) from UAV orthomosaics: a cascaded deep-learning pipeline with stratified validation across platforms, sensors, altitudes, and substrates
papers.abstract: Reliable demographic data are critical for seal population assessment and management, yet remain challenging to obtain from drone surveys without automated tools. Using data from harbor seal (Phoca vitulina) haulout surveys conducted in British Columbia, Canada, in 2023-2024, we developed and tested an automated pipeline that integrates detection, morphometric extraction, and size-class classification of seals into a single system. The pipeline combines cascaded DeepLabV3+ segmentation (water removal, colony-level seal detection, and individual body-contour refinement), principal component analysis (PCA)-based extraction of body length and maximum width, and three-class size-class determination based on body length (pups, juveniles, subadults/adults). We evaluated the pipeline on 2,483 manually annotated seals across four drone platforms (DJI Mavic 3 Thermal, Mavic 2 Pro, Mini 3 Pro and Mini 2), five substrate types, and two sensor modalities (RGB, thermal infrared). Aggregate detection F1 was 0.914. Orthomosaic geometric accuracy, quantified as the RMSE of calibration-rod length on the orthomosaic, ranged from 1.0 cm to 18.0 cm depending on the platform-altitude-substrate combination, a spread that aggregate metrics would mask. Relative to manual annotation on the same orthomosaics, automated RGB body lengths showed near-zero bias (-0.6 cm; RMSE = 12.5 cm), whereas automated thermal lengths were systematically shorter (bias -19.9 cm, RMSE = 24.1 cm), establishing the unsuitability of thermal imagery for automated quantitative pinniped morphometry. For RGB imagery, threshold classification by body length reached an overall accuracy (OA) of 78.7%; for individuals outside the uncertainty zones (defined as {+/-}2 x the geometric RMSE on calibration rods around each class boundary), OA reached 90.9%. Within the RGB subset, OA was 78.9% at 20 m altitude, declining to 75.0% at 40 m where geometric error dominated. The pipeline enables automated demographic monitoring of pinniped haulouts with quantitatively characterized uncertainty across survey conditions.

papers.title: Reconciling intrinsic and ecosystem water-use efficiency reveals physiological mechanisms underlying carbon-water coupling across biological scales
papers.abstract: Understanding how carbon-water coupling scales from leaves to ecosystems remains a major challenge because water-use efficiency (WUE) metrics integrate physiological, hydrological, and ecological processes. We integrated tree-ring width, triple stable isotopes ({delta}13C, {delta}18O and {delta}2H), eddy covariance (EC) observations, and a process-based model to investigate the drivers of intrinsic (iWUE) and ecosystem water-use efficiency (WUEeco) across biological scales in a mature Fagus sylvatica forest between 2004 and 2023. Modelled and isotope-derived iWUE were strongly correlated (r = 0.61, p < 0.05) and both indicated an approximately 20% long-term increase, consistent with increasing gross primary productivity. In contrast, WUEeco derived from EC was lower than model estimates and exhibited a positive trend not reproduced by the model. This divergence primarily reflected differences in biological representation and hydrological integration, as the single-species model underestimated ecosystem evapotranspiration by excluding co-occurring deciduous and evergreen species together with understory vegetation. Triple-isotope analyses showed that the long-term increase in iWUE was driven by enhanced photosynthetic assimilation rather than sustained stomatal closure, whereas {delta}18O and {delta}2H variability was mainly controlled by source-water dynamics. These findings provide a mechanistic framework for reconciling leaf- and ecosystem-scale WUE and improving predictions of forest carbon-water coupling under climate change.

papers.title: Trait-Based Selection of Annual Plant Species for Enhancing Ecosystem Functioning in Extensive Green Roof Systems: A Systematic Review
papers.abstract: Extensive green roofs are an important component of urban green infrastructure. However, harsh rooftop conditions, including shallow substrates, high temperatures and limited water availability, considerably restrict plant selection. Although extensive green roofs are traditionally dominated by succulent species, increasing attention has been directed towards annual plants because of their rapid establishment, developmental plasticity and potential contribution to vegetation diversity. This review aimed to identify annual plant species introduced on extensive green roofs and to characterize the functional traits most frequently associated with their establishment under rooftop conditions. In addition, the review examined the geographical distribution and methodological characteristics of existing studies and identified species with potential for application under temperate climatic conditions. A total of 22 studies published between 2015 and 2025 were analyzed, comprising 100 annual species representing 29 plant families. The reviewed studies showed a clear geographical bias towards Mediterranean and arid regions, whereas temperate climates were considerably underrepresented. Among species occurring in Central Europe, ruderal life strategies, drought avoidance, efficient dispersal mechanisms, low plant height and prolonged flowering were the most frequently observed functional characteristics, while seed mass and specific leaf area (SLA) exhibited substantial interspecific variation. These findings suggest that functional traits, rather than taxonomic affiliation alone, provide a useful framework for selecting annual species for extensive green roofs. The review also highlights the need for long-term studies conducted under temperate climatic conditions to improve evidence-based plant selection and support the development of resilient and multifunctional green roof vegetation.

papers.title: Density-Dependence and agricultural intensity affect host-parasite-parasitoid interactions in a bird-insect trophic system
papers.abstract: Agricultural intensification is a major cause of population declines in farmland birds and insects worldwide. While these declines are expected to disrupt trophic interactions through density-dependent cascading effects, examples outside of crop pest control or involving more than two trophic levels remain poorly documented. Here we quantify such cascading effects across three trophic levels involving a declining aerial insectivore, the Tree Swallow (Tachycineta bicolor), which breeding success decreases with agricultural intensity, Protocalliphora bird blowflies (Diptera: Calliphoridae) that parasitize its nestlings, and Nasonia parasitoid jewel wasps (Hymenoptera: Pteromalidae) that feed upon blowfly pupae within swallow nests. Agriculture intensity may affect each of these actors either directly via, for instance, toxicological effects from pesticide use, or indirectly through density-dependent trophic interactions, which can exacerbate or mitigate one another. Using Bayesian models within a causal inference framework, we quantified how nestling host density, meteorological conditions, and agricultural landscape context affect Nasonia parasitoid infestation of Protocalliphora pupae, and estimated Protocalliphora emergence success. Analyses were based on 3,340 Protocalliphora puparia collected from 248 Tree Swallow nests over a 16-year period (2004-2019) across a 10,200-km2 agricultural intensity gradient in Southern Quebec, Canada. Model predictions indicated that Protocalliphora emergence probability increased steeply with nestling host availability (i.e., nestling-days). Whereas Nasonia parasitoid infestation occurrence at the nest level increased with Protocalliphora host availability, the proportion of infested Protocalliphora pupae within nest decreased and led to a dilution effect at the individual level. Although Protocalliphora abundance within nests decreased with agricultural intensity, their emergence probability peaked in agrointensive landscapes. This increase was associated with reduced Nasonia infestation rates, suggesting that agricultural intensity indirectly mitigated parasitoid pressure on Protocalliphora host populations. Our results highlight how agricultural intensification can shape multitrophic interactions and life-history traits (emergence success and infestation rates) by simultaneously reducing host availability and weakening top-down control by parasitoids.

papers.title: A unified framework reveals how evolutionary scale and abundance weighting shape phylogenetic community structure
papers.abstract: Metrics describing phylogenetic community structure are widely used to infer assembly processes in biological communities, but existing metrics capture only fixed phylogenetic scales and provide limited control over how rare and abundant taxa influence ecological patterns. Here we introduce q-weighted interpolated mean phylogenetic distance (qiMPD), a framework that continuously interpolates between broad evolutionary divergence and nearest-taxon distance while incorporating tunable abundance weighting. Applied to 3661 wastewater microbiomes, qiMPD revealed that abundance weighting had little effect on broad-scale phylogenetic dispersion but strongly altered local phylogenetic structure. Null-model analyses showed that within-community signals of phylogenetic overdispersion and clustering, and between-community signals of phylogenetic divergence and convergence, emerged at different combinations of phylogenetic locality and abundance weighting. Thus, the qiMPD framework enables phylogenetic scale- and abundance-resolved inference of community assembly. It is implemented in the Python package qdiv version 4.2.0.

papers.title: Epidemiological model selection unravels the molecular processes of antiviral resistance from experimental phytoplankton-virus dynamics
papers.abstract: Phytoplankton-virus interactions are pivotal in understanding the intertwined dynamics of these key players of the global carbon cycle. Although antiviral resistance is the main hypothesis to solve the apparent paradox of their coexistence, identifying its molecular determinisms and mechanisms, as well as their dynamical consequences, remains challenging. By combining hypotheses about such determinisms and mechanisms, we designed 36 dynamical models and fitted them to experimental infection kinetics in a pioneering selection model approach. Through such a multiple hypotheses testing, we identified that resistance in the model species Ostreococcus tauri is most likely to be predominantly intracellular, to control lysis through budding, and to be acquired by phenotypic plasticity. We further showed that viral kinetics are strongly impacted by both the antiviral resistance's molecular determinants and virions' inactivation through attachment to lysis detritus, as the latter generates a key negative feedback loop during the 'bust' stage of the interaction dynamics.

papers.title: Environmental variability alters and obscures fisheries-induced evolution
papers.abstract: Shifts in predation and human harvest often coincide with changes in life history trait distributions in prey populations. These changes may arise via evolution or plasticity, and extrinsic environmental effects may affect such traits. This complexity prompts questions about how trait distributions are shaped by multiple factors' interactions. We hypothesized that food availability and climate affect both the magnitude, and mechanism (evolution vs. plasticity), by which traits change in response to harvest's intensity and size selectivity. We tested these hypotheses using individual-based bioenergetic population models allowing both plasticity and evolution. We exposed genetically diverse fish populations to gradients of productivity and stochasticity in food availability, crossed with gradients of selective or nonselective fishing mortality. Food availability shaped traits both plastically and evolutionarily, and modulated how harvesting influenced those responses. Food effects can suppress harvest impacts altogether, or obscure evolution's effects on phenotypes. However, when climatic factors shape food-driven changes by affecting both fish and their prey, either synergistic or antagonistic interactions can emerge between food variation and harvest in determining phenotype distributions. Our research suggests that understanding consumer-resource dynamics, and climatic processes shaping them, is essential to interpreting how harvest can shape traits relevant to population viability and fisheries sustainability.

papers.title: Mapping potential for human encounters with dangerous large mammals across a community-led Wildlife Management Area in southern Tanzania based on overlapping signs of recent activity
papers.abstract: This study examined the spatial distribution of potential human encounters with dangerous large mammals in and adjacent to the Ifakara-Lupiro-Mang'ula Wildlife Management Area (ILUMA WMA) and Nyerere National Park (NNP) in southern Tanzania. Using published survey data collected over one year, this secondary analysis focused on four potentially dangerous large mammals: elephant (Loxodonta africana), buffalo (Syncerus caffer), hippopotamus (Hippopotamus amphibius) and hyena (Crocuta crocuta). Potential encounter risk was estimated using overlap indices based on co-occurrence of signs of wildlife and human activities. Potential encounter risk was found to be concentrated around readily identifiable foci within the study area and differed between species and distinguishable human livelihood activities. Potential for encountering the two most apparently important dangerous animals, elephant and buffalo, was closely associated with authorized fishing camps within the ILUMA WMA and the ecotone between substantially disturbed and largely intact natural land cover. The greatest potential for encountering hippopotamus occurred largely around two river beds, while hyena encounter potential was more closely associated with established villages and converted lands close to the western boundary of the ILUMA WMA. These new maps of hazard and risk suggest that effective human-wildlife conflict (HWC) mitigation in this WMA is unlikely to arise from any stand-alone intervention, but from targeted actions that reduce spatiotemporal overlap between people and wildlife by keeping them apart and/or protecting them against each other. Overall, this study demonstrates that mapping potential encounter risk based on spatiotemporal overlap of indirect activity indicators like tracks, spoor and signs provides a proactive and statistically powerful way to identify where hazardous encounters are most likely to occur, offering considerable advantages over retrospective assessments of much sparser observations of actual realised conflict events after they have already occurred. This new spatial risk mapping approach provides a framework for shifting management from reactive responses after conflict occurs towards proactive prevention.

papers.title: A lightweight deep-learning detector for the real-time monitoring of the invasive frogs Rhinella marina and Polypedates leucomystax
papers.abstract: Early detection of invasive species is critical to efficiently managing biological invasions. Passive acoustic monitoring combined with deep learning has become an effective tool for identifying invasive anurans from their species-specific mating calls. In practice, however, these systems still depend on manually retrieving recordings and running inference on a dedicated workstation, which delays detection at invasion fronts, especially on remote islands where frequent travel is impractical. Here, we present a lightweight convolutional neural network for detecting Rhinella marina and Polypedates leucomystax that can be used with low-power microcontrollers, enabling continuous, real-time monitoring of these invasive species. Our model achieved a mean invasive-species F1 of 0.87 with precision higher than 0.88 for both species, comparable to the performance of substantially larger models at a fraction of the model size. Cross-domain evaluation confirmed reliable detection on two out-of-training locations: Iriomote Island, Japan, and on an independent dataset from Australia, demonstrating generalization across recording conditions and biogeographic contexts, albeit with local threshold calibration for P. leucomystax at Iriomote. Our results demonstrate that effective acoustic detection of invasive species is feasible on self-contained, battery-powered devices, removing the dependence on server infrastructure and enabling autonomous early warning systems in remote protected areas.

papers.title: Dark diversity reveals assembly constraints across trophic levels in large-scale grassland restoration
papers.abstract: 1. Grassland biodiversity restoration efforts have largely focused on re-establishing diverse plant communities, with less attention paid to higher trophic levels such as invertebrates. 2. We established a controlled, field-scale restoration experiment across twelve lowland grassland sites in Switzerland in close collaboration with farmers. We manipulated seed addition (hay transfer, directly harvested seeds, or multiplied seed mixtures) and soil disturbance (shallow or deep tillage), with treatments applied to meadows covering, on average, 0.5 ha. Four to six years after restoration, we quantified the components of species richness change (lost, persisting, gained from site surroundings, and gained from donors), and estimated dark diversity (species that are absent from a location but could potentially occur there) for plants, Auchenorrhyncha and Orthoptera. 3. Compared to plants, invertebrates exhibited greater species turnover, with higher proportions of species lost and gained from the surroundings, but much lower contributions from the donor meadows. However, species persistence was high across taxa. Restoration operations strongly influenced components of species richness change in plants but had weaker effects on invertebrates. In particular, multiplied seed mixtures + deep tillage had the highest proportion of plant species not transferred, suggesting that many species in the seed mixture were poorly suited to local conditions. In both plants and Auchenorrhyncha, components of species richness change were strongly mediated by site characteristics, with initial species richness in both receiver and donor emerging as the strongest predictors. 4. Within each taxonomic group, 41% of species not transferred from the donor belonged to the dark diversity, suggesting substantial unrealized restoration potential. Restoration operations impacted dark diversity for plants and Auchenorrhyncha but not for Orthoptera. In plants, dark diversity was substantially lower under multiplied seed mixtures + deep tillage than under other treatments. The probability of a species belonging to dark diversity was associated with specific leaf area in plants and initial relative abundance in Auchenorrhyncha. 5. Synthesis and applications. Components of species richness change were influenced by both restoration operations and site characteristics, with their relative importance varying among taxa, underscoring the need for multi-taxon restoration strategies.

papers.title: When blood is not thicker than water: Social information landscapes offset the food-fear trade-off in habitat selection decisions
papers.abstract: 1. Group foraging reduces the risks associated with foraging: larger groups dilute individual predation risk, allow group members to share the costs of vigilance, and provide a social structure for exchanging information about predators. The benefits of shared social information over simple safety in numbers should depend on the relationships among group members. Consequently, group composition should affect the selection of risky and safe habitats in social species. 2. We asked whether relationships among elk (Cervus canadensis) group members moving together influence their selection of risky habitats more than grouping alone. We tested three hypotheses. The familiarity hypothesis predicts that elk with close social ties are most likely to select risky habitats together. The inclusive fitness hypothesis predicts that the closest genetic relatives are most likely to select risky habitats together. The dilution hypothesis predicts that familiarity and genetic relationships do not influence habitat selection, with all group foraging benefits derived from proximity to others. 3. We used integrated Step Selection Analysis to test whether the identity of the closest group members influenced habitat selection. We tested whether the relationship of the nearest elk--either genetic or social--incentivized selection of risky habitat more than proximity to the nearest elk. 4. Group foraging clearly reduced risk, with elk more likely to select risky habitat when near others. Elk were also more likely to select risky habitats when near closer relatives, albeit with considerable variation among individuals. However, familiarity had a large and consistent effect: elk were far more likely to select risky habitats when near socially familiar group members. 5. Our results suggest that information shared within foraging groups, especially between socially familiar individuals, may lower the risks associated with habitat selection. Similarly, the benefits of reliable social information for reducing risk likely incentivizes the formation of stronger social ties within foraging groups. This positive feedback between social familiarity and habitat selection could thereby increase access to profitable habitats that are otherwise too risky, cementing what we term the social information landscape as a key driver of movement and habitat selection.

papers.title: A modelling challenge to improve preparedness for highly pathogenicavian influenza epidemics: objectives, design and synthetic datageneration
papers.abstract: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) is among the most significant disease threats to poultry worldwide. Modelling challenges, where independent teams address a common epidemiological scenario, can support the development of response capabilities and strengthen communication between modellers and risk managers. Despite the established benefits of these exercises, they remain uncommon in animal health, and none have previously addressed avian influenza. Here Jolly Island, an artificial landscape of 9160 poultry farms with five production types, was developed and seeded with stochastic HPAI epidemics that ran their course over a three-to-four month period. From January through April 2026, 45 registered teams across five continents investigated a selected synthetic epidemic, producing probabilistic forecasts, inferring transmission drivers, and evaluating counterfactual control policies. Here the objectives, design choices, and data generation of the HPAI Modelling Challenge are described in full, covering transmission processes, surveillance system operations, and control strategy implementation, along with the selected epidemic trajectory, the narrative situation reports supplied to the teams at each phase, and the complete phase-specific datasets released to them. As the opening paper of this special issue, here is provided the foundation upon which all subsequent contributions, where teams document their approaches and analyses, are built.

papers.title: Landscape restoration strategies differ in their predicted benefits for species persistence
papers.abstract: Global biodiversity recovery demands restoration at landscape scales, where ecological outcomes are shaped not only by habitat amount but also spatial arrangement. Alternative landscape restoration strategies can increase habitat amount, improve quality, and alter configuration in fundamentally different ways and may therefore vary in their efficiency. Here, we conceptualise five landscape restoration strategies and use a spatially explicit metapopulation framework to compare their ability to increase predicted species persistence across heterogeneous landscapes and trait space defined by dispersal ability and specialisation. We find that restoration outcomes are strongly trait-dependent, with restoration of existing degraded habitats yielding the highest benefits - particularly for specialists. Improvement of the landscape matrix to create low-quality habitat primarily benefits generalists, while strategies creating new habitat patches or enlarging patches provide more consistent but modest gains. These results reveal fundamental trade-offs among restoration strategies and highlight the utility of trait-explicit approaches to inform their implementation and evaluation.

papers.title: Temporal stasis in three facets of biodiversity reveals mechanisms of community assembly across elevation gradients
papers.abstract: Understanding spatial and temporal variation in community composition is central to protecting and monitoring biodiversity. Similarity in the composition of two communities decreases along spatial and temporal gradients, a relationship known as distance decay. Comparing distance-decay relationships across taxonomic, functional, and bioclimatic facets of diversity provides a means of interrogating niche-based versus neutral influences on community assembly. Furthermore, the context in which these facets yield overlapping or complementary information about global change impacts remains poorly understood. In this study, we examined spatiotemporal distance-decay relationships for taxonomic, functional, and bioclimatic facets of alpine plant diversity leveraging elevation gradients on five peaks in the White Mountains, California, USA, sampled at 3-4 time points between 2007 and 2024. Using multivariate Bayesian beta regression models, we estimated the slopes of elevation distance decay over multiple surveys and across taxonomic, functional and bioclimatic diversity to understand how spatial distance-decay relationships are changing through time and across different facets of diversity. We found strong spatial distance decay of taxonomic similarity across all peaks, with the highest elevation peak showing the strongest decay. Functional and bioclimatic similarities decayed more weakly than taxonomic similarity, suggesting environmental filtering shapes trait and niche distributions. Critically, spatial decay patterns showed no temporal signal across facets of diversity, indicating community stasis rather than biotic homogenization or differentiation. This study adds further evidence that xeric alpine plant communities are resisting climate change impacts through time.

papers.title: Domestication, spread, and improvement have shaped biological nitrogen fixation traits in Zea taxa
papers.abstract: Synthetic nitrogen fertilizers enhance maize (Zea mays ssp. mays) productivity but impose substantial environmental and economic costs. Some Mexican maize landraces support biological nitrogen fixation (BNF) in aerial root mucilage, raising the question of how much variation exists in this trait and how domestication, geographic spread, and improvement have shaped BNF-related traits across Zea in the Americas. We evaluated aerial root traits and BNF capacity across the maize domestication continuum using 60 Zea accessions grown in field experiments over two years under low-N conditions. Some accessions of wild Zea, landraces from Mexico and South America, and improved varieties had elevated nitrogen derived from the atmosphere (%Ndfa), ranging from 20 to 40%; some of these also had greater %Ndfa than typical improved varieties. Spread and improvement appear to have significantly reduced the number of aerial root-bearing nodes, with wild Zea and Mexican landraces consistently producing more. Nevertheless, the proportion of nitrogen derived from the atmosphere (%Ndfa) does not vary systematically across the domestication continuum. Thus, crop evolution shaped aerial root phenotypes more than associative BNF capacity. The persistence of substantial within-group variation indicates that the genetic potential for enhanced BNF remains within the Zea gene pool, providing opportunities to encourage and improve nitrogen use efficiency in maize cropping systems.

papers.title: Carabid beetle communities along a gradient of agroecological systems: disentangling the roles of pesticides and soil tillage
papers.abstract: The potential of alternative agricultural systems, such as organic or conservation agriculture, for biodiversity restoration has been widely investigated. However, variability of practices within each of these two categories of agricultural system has rarely been accounted for. Furthermore, these systems have most often been studied separately, isolating either organic or conservation agriculture (itself often reduced to a soil tillage reduction), and rarely analyzing these systems side by side. This study attempts to disentangle these multiple interrelationships by sampling carabid beetles in a network of 48 commercial Belgian farms including organic agriculture (OA), conservation agriculture (CA), farms combining the two approaches (OCA) and farms applying conventional practices (CVA). In each farm, we sampled carabids using pitfall and emergence traps in one winter cereal field and collected a detailed description of crop management practices. We found that community composition was primarily structured by seasonality early in the season (March, April) followed by convergence (May, June) driven by the aggregation of the most dominant species. Based on agroecosystem classification, organic certification (i.e., the absence of synthetic pesticide use) exerted a twofold stronger effect than application of conservation agriculture principles (i.e., reduced or no soil tillage) on carabid beetle community composition. Notably, OCA supported carabid assemblages that were structurally distinct from those of CA and CVA. Furthermore, carabid communities associated with OA differed significantly in composition from those of CVA. Observed and estimated species richness were also significantly higher in OCA than in CA and CVA, while OA differed from CVA only for observed richness. Beyond differences among agricultural systems, community responses were associated with specific management practices, which explained nearly a quarter of the compositional variation with significant influence of the duration since organic conversion and the frequency of synthetic pesticide application. Carabid abundances were negatively affected by synthetic pesticides and moldboard ploughing, whereas richness was more strongly related to the time since conversion to OA, cover crops, and organic amendments. Overall, these results position synthetic inputs and time since conversion as the main filters over carabid communities. Our study highlights the importance of jointly considering system level analyses and detailed management practices to better understand the complex relationships between agricultural practices and carabid communities.

papers.title: Fluffy nests and bloody parasites: feather lining does not mitigate bird blow flies infestations
papers.abstract: Feathers incorporated into bird nests are thought to provide multiple benefits, including thermal insulation and protection against nest-dwelling ectoparasites. For instance, in Swallows, it has been suggested that feathers influence infestations by Protocalliphora blow flies either by acting as a physical barrier between larvae and nestlings or through chemical compounds associated with preen oil. However, empirical evidence for an antiparasitic effect of feathers remains equivocal. Using 1,100 naturally infested Tree Swallow (Tachycineta bicolor) nests collected from a nest-box study system monitored in southern Quebec, Canada, between 2004 and 2018, we tested whether nest mass and feather abundance influenced hematophagous ectoparasites (Protocalliphora spp.) loads. We further assessed whether feather abundance directly affected body size using measurements of 1,513 P. sialia puparia, and emergence success using data from 961 Protocalliphora spp. puparia. Nest mass was positively associated with feather abundance, and both variables showed very weak positive relationships with parasite abundance. Feather abundance was unrelated to puparium size nor parasite emergence success. Our results provide no support for an anti-parasitic effect of feather lining within Tree Swallow nests. Using one of the largest datasets assembled to date on feather-lined nests and avian blow flies, we found no evidence that feather abundance impairs Protocalliphora density, development or emergence success. However, our findings do not preclude potential effects of feathers on other ectoparasites or microorganisms with different life histories. Future studies simultaneously monitoring multiple parasite taxa (such as fleas, mites, or bacteria) may therefore be needed to fully evaluate the ecological consequences of feather lining within avian nests.

papers.title: SELECTIVE SURVIVAL OF AVIAN ECTOPARASITES IN AGROINTENSIVE HABITATS AND SUBSEQUENT EFFECTS ON HOST SELECTION BY PARASITOIDS
papers.abstract: Morphological variation in insects can indicate responses to habitat change and land use intensification, with potential consequences for trophic interactions. In insect host-parasitoid systems, host body is often a key determinant of offspring development and emergence success, as well as parasitoid host-selection behavior. Yet, most studies in agricultural landscapes have focused on size variation in crop-associated insects (i.e.: pests, pollinators and enemies), leaving those relying on non-crop resources largely unexplored. Here, we investigated how agroenvironmental contexts and trophic resource availability influence puparial size in Protocalliphora sialia (Diptera: Calliphoridae), an obligate hematophagous ectoparasite of Tree Swallow (Tachycineta bicolor) nestlings. We further tested whether puparial size affects emergence probability and risk of parasitoidism by Nasonia spp. (Hymenoptera: Pteromalidae) jewel wasps. Using 1,513 P. sialia puparia from 88 nests within a nest-box monitoring system spanning a 10,200-km^2 east-west intensification gradient in southern Quebec, Canada, we evaluated how agrointensive contexts, avian host availability, and ectoparasite densities influence puparial size, parasitoidism risk, and emergence success. The agricultural context appears to shape puparial size through survival biases and/or altered growth rates. In agroextensive contexts (i.e.: pastures, forages with high tree cover), where Protocalliphora are more numerous, P. sialia puparia were smaller and exhibited greater size variation. Conversely, in agrointensive environments (maize and soybeans monocultures with higher doses of pesticides), where Protocalliphora are fewer, small individuals were underrepresented, suggesting a selective mortality in P. sialia population. However, puparial size explained less than 10% of the variation in emergence or parasitism, likely reflecting consistently high parasitic pressure from Nasonia wasps, which infested 50-90% of puparia, depending on site and year. Our findings highlight the importance of selective mortality in structuring trait distributions and modulating multi-trophic interactions in human-modified landscapes.

papers.title: Baseline growth rate shapes pollutant impacts in aquatic environments: Evidence from antibiotic responses in the harmful cyanobacterium Microcystis
papers.abstract: Hormesis is an important consideration in chemical risk assessment across most aquatic environments. Evidence suggests that hormetic responses are shaped by organismal physiological processes. Accordingly, predictions of hormesis under environmentally realistic conditions should account for physiological traits. Yet the role of these traits remains largely unexplored. This study investigated how baseline growth rate modulates antibiotic responses in the harmful cyanobacterium Microcystis and the underlying mechanisms. Results showed that at an antibiotic concentration of 200 ng L-1 (representing environmental concentration levels), slow-growing Microcystis populations exhibited an obvious growth enhancement more than 4-fold greater than that of fast-growing populations, and this enhancement was positively correlated with cellular reserves. A baseline growth rate below 0.19 day-1 emerged as the threshold below which hormetic responses were consistently observed. This study provides pioneering insights into how organisms' physiological states influence pollutant-induced hormetic responses in aquatic environments. Our findings point to a central principle for extrapolation that laboratory-derived toxicological responses may not translate directly to the field unless key physiological traits of the organisms are explicitly considered. In this regard, baseline growth rate and energy reserves may be key physiological traits for reliably predicting toxic effects at the population level. This study also makes an initial attempt to conceptualize a physiology-anchored framework for strengthening risk assessment of low-level emerging contaminants.

papers.title: Hierarchical permutation entropy regression identifies decadal decline in the intrinsic predictability of butterfly populations
papers.abstract: Short-term population dynamics are shaped by both external environmental stochasticity and endogenous ecological dynamics. The extent to which population trajectories maintain predictable temporal structure reflects underlying determinism and sets limits on inherent forecastability. Permutation entropy quantifies this intrinsic predictability using the relative frequency of short fluctuation motifs. However, requirements for long timeseries have restricted ecological applications. Here, I introduce a Bayesian hierarchical regression framework, incorporating entropy-neutral priors, that estimates expected permutation entropy from shorter, spatially-distributed ecological datasets. I validate the approach's capacity to detect the impact of increasing environmental variance through simulations. Applied to four decades of UK butterfly data, the approach identified increasing permutation entropy across 35 species, consistent with an increasing role of stochastic weather events. Outlier weather events did not have a consistent relationship with permutation entropy, highlighting the potential for environmental forcing to both disrupt and constrain trajectories. With this flexible approach, permutation entropy offers complementary perspectives on longstanding questions around forecasting and population dynamics.

papers.title: Functional Diversity of Reef Fishes in the Veracruz Reef System National Park, SW Gulf of Mexico
papers.abstract: Reef fish assemblages in the Veracruz Reef System National Park (VRSNP) are strongly structured along a pronounced north-south gradient, where environmental conditions, urban proximity, and protection levels interact to shape functional diversity and ecosystem functioning. This gradient creates contrasting ecological conditions between northern and southern reefs, providing a natural framework for evaluating how spatial variation influences resilience. Using a stationary visual census across ten reefs distributed latitudinally, we quantified functional entities based on six ecological traits and calculated functional richness, redundancy, over-redundancy, vulnerability, specialization, and originality. A two-way permutational ANOVA and redundancy analysis were used to detect spatial and temporal patterns and to link functional indices with environmental features. The southern sector displayed the most intense functional shifts. Nearshore southern reefs, strongly exposed to sedimentation, nutrient loading, and physical disturbance, exhibited reduced functional richness, fewer functional entities, and high functional vulnerability, indicating strong environmental filtering. Over time, these reefs shifted toward generalist-dominated assemblages with rising redundancy, suggesting functional convergence. In contrast, southern offshore reefs supported higher taxonomic and functional richness, buffered by greater habitat complexity and distance from shore, although they showed declining redundancy, likely reflecting sensitivity to regional climatic disturbances. In the northern sector, the gradient was moderated by effective protection, which reshaped functional configurations. Nearshore protected reefs such as Isla Sacrificios and Isla de Enmedio maintained high redundancy, low vulnerability, and high biomass of large-bodied fishes, resembling offshore systems rather than disturbed southern nearshore reefs. The northern offshore reef (Isla Verde) shared some of these attributes but exhibited temporal declines in richness, signaling emerging vulnerabilities along the gradient. Functional originality and specialization aligned with benthic states across the gradient, particularly where macroalgal or calcareous substrates prevailed. Overall, the north-south gradient is the primary axis of functional organization in VRSNP, revealing that resilience emerges from the interplay among reef geomorphology, urban influence, and governance effectiveness.

papers.title: Conceptualising and quantifying phenological plasticity through latent responses to seasonal environmental progression
papers.abstract: Quantifying how individuals adjust the seasonal timings of life-history events (i.e. their phenology) in response to seasonal environmental conditions is fundamental to predicting impacts of changing seasonality. However, the current standard approach of inferring phenological responses by directly analysing observed event dates relies on foundational assumptions that could be invalidated by changing seasonality, and excludes individuals that do not express focal events, potentially generating misleading inferences. To overcome these limitations, we devised a Phenological Threshold Model (PTM) that conceptualizes phenological events as switches between discrete life-history states and primarily estimates variation in underlying latent dynamic responses to seasonal progression, from which event dates secondarily arise. We demonstrate that the PTM can accurately retrieve simulated parameter values, including given incomplete seasonal field observations. Application to multi-year data on annual breeding in black-legged kittiwakes (Rissa tridactyla) demonstrated substantial among-individual variation in latent responses to seasonally varying environmental drivers, and associated daily probabilities that individuals will initiate breeding, revealing how annual distributions of breeding dates and proportions of non-breeders jointly arise. We thereby formalise a new conceptual and statistical framework for quantifying the potential for, and constraints on, rapid plastic and micro-evolutionary changes in phenology in changing seasonal climatic and environmental regimes.

papers.title: Intermediate phenotypic heterogeneity creates an optimal coexistence window in bacteria-phage communities
papers.abstract: Phenotypic heterogeneity can expand ecological niche space even within a genetically homogeneous population. Recent experiments showed that growth-rate heterogeneity in a clonal bacterial host can stabilize coexistence among multiple phages. Yet this discovery leaves unresolved whether increasing host heterogeneity monotonically promotes coexistence. Here we show that it does not. Using a trait-based bacteria--phage coexistence framework, we find that phage richness is maximized at an intermediate scale of host growth-rate heterogeneity, determined by the match between host phenotypic dispersion and phage niche width. Our results show that optimal phage diversity emerges from an ecological trade-off between two competing effects: increasing phenotypic heterogeneity enables niche differentiation but eventually reduces the host abundance in the preferred niche of each phage. Therefore, our findings predict that experimentally increasing host growth-rate variance at a fixed mean growth rate should produce a nonmonotonic phage richness response, providing a quantitative principle for how intraspecific phenotypic variation shapes biodiversity in microbial ecosystems.

papers.title: Correcting and georeferencing natural history occurrence records with calibrated uncertainty
papers.abstract: 1. Occurrence records underpin biodiversity analyses, but their coordinates are often erroneous or missing. Misplaced coordinates distort environmental predictors and range estimates used in conservation assessment. Existing tools flag suspect records or georeference locality text, but rarely correct coordinates, provide calibrated uncertainty, or quantify downstream consequences. 2. We present GeoMend, a deterministic, rule-based method that flags and corrects suspect coordinates and georeferences records lacking coordinates from locality text, assigning each a precision tier or uncertainty radius. It uses no machine learning or artificial intelligence. We evaluate it against expert coordinates for 16,913 records and 736 species on Hispaniola, compare georeferencers using 5,000 localities from 72 countries, and measure changes in environmental predictors and the extent of occurrence. 3. On held-out Hispaniola records, GeoMend flags 92% of coordinates more than 5 km from expert truth, versus 27% for CoordinateCleaner. Among the accepted corrections with paired coordinates, the median error falls from 2.19 to 0.82 km, and 68% of the complete held-out pairs improve. On records placed by both GeoMend and GEOLocate that also have original coordinates, the median error is 0.67 km for GeoMend versus 10.69 km for GEOLocate. For records lacking coordinates, evaluated uncertainty radii contain expert truth about 92% of the time in well-supported gazetteer classes. Correction reduces the mean standardized environmental distance from expert truth by 38% and moves the extent of occurrence toward expert truth by a median of 8% (mean of 79%). Corrections and newly georeferenced records give 17 Hispaniola species their first range estimate. 4. On the global benchmark, GeoMend is more accurate than GPT-4o for two-thirds of the records placed by all four comparators, with median errors of 4.4 and 10.8 km, respectively. Applied to Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF) records lacking coordinates, it places records from 82,180 previously unmapped species across 233 countries, ranging from precise locality interpretations to administrative centroids. Automated placement makes the global backlog more approachable, while explicit tiers distinguish uses supported by precise and coarse coordinates. Further georeferencing requires regional expertise to combine automated placement with local knowledge.

papers.title: Scents for safe sex: a volatile sex pheromone promotes outbreeding in a parasitoid wasp with severe genetic load
papers.abstract: When mating among genetically related individuals results in inbreeding depression, various behaviors and life-history traits evolve to favor outbreeding. Long-range sexual communication following natal dispersal is one such adaptation. In parasitoid wasps with single-locus complementary sex determination (sl-CSD), inbreeding increases the production of unviable or sterile diploid males. Mastrus ridens is such a species, with a genetic load underpinned by sl-CSD, combined with a high potential for sibmating because siblings emerge in close proximity from the same host and become sexually active shortly after emergence. With this context in mind, we investigated the mate-finding strategy of M. ridens using complementary behavioral, chemical, and electrophysiological approaches. Wind-tunnel bioassays and field experiments showed that males orient toward virgin females and, to a lesser extent, mated females. This attraction from a distance appeared to be the sole form of conspecific attraction. Chemical analyses using static and dynamic headspace sampling and solvent extracts, followed by GC-MS, revealed several potential pheromonal candidates, including methyl 6-methylsalicylate. This compound elicited reproducible antennal responses in males in GC-EAD recordings. Altogether, our results suggest that mate finding in M. ridens is guided by a volatile sex pheromone emitted by females, with methyl 6-methylsalicylate as one putative component. Such mate-finding mechanisms promote outbreeding and may explain the low proportion of unfit diploid males observed in natural populations. Surprisingly, chemical analyses suggested that males also emit this compound, whereas neither males nor females showed behavioral responses to males. This apparent discrepancy suggests that attraction may depend on a more complex pheromonal signal and opens further avenues for investigation.

papers.title: Piloting floral-visitor assemblages: Camera-based monitoring in Physoplexis comosa (Campanulaceae), a cliff-dwelling Eastern Alpine endemic Physoplexis comosa (Campanulaceae)
papers.abstract: Understanding floral visitor dynamics along elevational gradients is essential for assessing potential implications for pollen limitation and population genetic processes in fragmented populations of cliff-dwelling alpine endemics. Physoplexis comosa (Campanulaceae) is a chasmophytic paleoendemic restricted to vertical rock faces on dolomitic and limestone bedrock from 200 to 2,800 m a.s.l. The species exhibits a specific floral morphology with fused corolla apices, basal openings for nectar access, and secondary pollen presentation, yet its functional floral visitor assemblage has remained poorly characterized across the species' elevational range. In this pilot study, we tested a two-tier camera-monitoring setup combining action cameras for diurnal monitoring with Raspberry Pi-based systems equipped with IR illumination for combined diurnal and nocturnal recording. We conducted monitoring across five elevational sites (1,480 to 2,400 m a.s.l.) in the Eastern Alps. Recorded video material was downsampled and annotated using the Addax platform alongside manual cross-validation to record physical contact events. Preliminary results confirm the technical feasibility of continuous monitoring in steep terrain and suggest possible elevational variation in diurnal visitors, alongside nocturnal activity by Geometridae moths. Camera-based observations provided higher functional resolution and revealed a different visitor assemblage than previous eDNA metabarcoding trials. This proof-of-concept establishes a methodological foundation for forthcoming multi-day monitoring campaigns and complements ongoing studies of the mating system and population-genetic analyses.

papers.title: From Recovery to Risk: Intensifying ENSO Events Drive Extirpation Risk in a Marine Predator
papers.abstract: Climate change poses a major threat to marine mammal populations, many of which remain vulnerable after years of overexploitation during the 17th to 20th centuries. Extreme climate events have grown in both frequency and severity in recent decades, and this trend is projected to accelerate under continued greenhouse gas emissions. Here, we assess how this intensification affects a top marine predator at the epicentre of extreme El Nino events - the Peruvian population of Otaria byronia (South American sea lion). We first apply a Bayesian population model that best predicts observed population dynamics to reconstruct female O. byronia population trends, estimate vital rates, and evaluate the effects of environmental drivers on survival and reproduction. We then use the same model to project extirpation risk under multiple future climate scenarios reflecting anticipated increases in both the intensity and frequency of extreme El Nino events. Our reconstruction reveals that the Peruvian O. byronia population has shown considerable resilience to episodic El Nino events over the past quarter-century, likely sustained by high female survival during normal and favourable years. However, under a scenario of moderate increases in El Nino frequency and intensity, the probability of extirpation over the next 50 years is 83.4% higher than under current conditions. As disturbance regimes intensify globally, we suggest that resilience-oriented management frameworks, grounded in species-specific demographic data and environmental context, as demonstrated here, will be essential for safeguarding marine mammal populations against an increasingly volatile climate.

papers.title: Zoogeochemical engineers: Galapagos giant tortoises link terrestrial and freshwater ecosystems through sediment transport and nutrient dynamics
papers.abstract: Animal movements can transport materials across ecosystem boundaries, while simultaneously modifying habitats through physical engineering. We integrated GPS telemetry, camera trapping, sediment measurements and physicochemical sampling of ponds on Santa Cruz Island, Galapagos, to evaluate how giant tortoises connect and shape terrestrial and freshwater ecosystems. Telemetry revealed 2,254 visits by 21 tortoises to 12 ponds, with visits lasting up to 21.38 h and showing strong seasonal and diel variation, while camera traps showed peak pond use in January and during early morning and late afternoon. Greater tortoise abundance was associated with higher ammonium, dissolved organic carbon and total phosphorus concentrations, while ponds with persistently greater tortoise abundance had higher total suspended solids. Departing tortoises carried a mean 505.9 g of sediment, yielding a conservative potential export of 8.20 kg per tortoise per year and tens of tonnes annually. These findings identify giant tortoises as mobile zoogeochemical engineers linking terrestrial and freshwater ecosystems through physical and biogeochemical pathways.

papers.title: Edge-enhanced disruptive camouflage is contrast dependent in VR environments
papers.abstract: In camouflage research, field studies provide ecological validity but lack experimental control, and computer-based experimental studies have the opposite issue. Virtual reality (VR) systems could potentially allow researchers to have both experimental control and ecological validity. Here we develop a VR environment using Unreal Engine and present it via a head-mounted display (HMD). The HMD affords binocular depth and therefore a more ecologically valid, three-dimensional environment, whilst still maintaining experimental control. Disruptive camouflage interferes with depth-based cues, making it a good candidate for testing within a VR environment. Disruptively camouflaged moth-like targets were presented to human surrogate predators, and their survivability was measured. We show that VR can be used to measure camouflage effectiveness by replicating existing findings showing that edge-enhanced disruptive camouflage (EE-DC) is more effective than disruptive camouflage (DC) alone. Furthermore, we extend these findings to show that the effectiveness of EE-DC is modulated by the relative contrast of the disruptive patches. Specifically, it is more effective when the contrast difference between the patches is low. Additionally, we considered edge-enhancement in isolation and found that it still provided a camouflage benefit even without a DC component. Search paradigms within an immersive VR experimental framework offer a unique opportunity to evaluate camouflage theory in a rigorous, yet ecologically grounded manner.

papers.title: Forward time-series causal inference based on forest weights and conditional dependence
papers.abstract: Unveiling directional causality in complex, high-dimensional dynamical systems remains a fundamental challenge. Conventional nonparametric approaches, such as Convergent Cross Mapping, require computationally intensive surrogate tests and frequently yield false-positive detections under strong coupling due to generalized synchronization. Here, we present F-CODEC (Forest-weighted Conditional Dependence Coefficient), a forward-looking causal discovery framework integrating generalized random forests with adaptive rank conditioning. Nonparametrically conditioning on the target variable's intrinsic delay coordinates systematically neutralizes shared manifold representations, suppressing false positives without surrogate data. Furthermore, an analytical time-series threshold allows instant, rigorous hypothesis testing directly from raw observations. We demonstrate F-CODEC's resilience against generalized synchronization and high-dimensional noise across canonical chaotic benchmarks and multi-species network motifs. Applying F-CODEC to historical lynx-hare cycles resolves delayed trophic forcing, while in-situ IoT honeybee monitoring captures real-time microclimate-acoustic causal surges preceding colony-level behavioral events. F-CODEC establishes a practical, scalable, and surrogate-free tool for causal discovery in nonlinear dynamical systems.
